chapters.title: CHAPTER THREE: THE LAWYER IN THE DUNES

spans.text: The summer Solei came back from UNC, she came back different.

Not in the way of someone who had changed their mind about things, more in the way of someone who had finished being uncertain about them. She walked off the ferry with the same duffel bag she'd always had and the same sunglasses she'd borrowed from Olivia three summers ago and never returned, but there was something in how she moved through the dock crowd that was new. Unhurried in a way that wasn't patience. More like she had decided the world would arrange itself around her, eventually, and she was prepared to wait.

Victoria noticed it from the parking lot, where she was leaning against the Jeep with a paper coffee cup that had gone cold. She noticed it and filed it, the way she filed most things, without announcement, for later.
You look different,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: she said, when Solei reached her.
I cut my hair.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: That's not it.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Solei put her duffel in the back of the Jeep.
I had a very good year,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: she said.
I'll tell you about it when I've had actual coffee.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Olivia had opened the Ginger Mae at seven-fifteen, which was the time it always opened, which was also the time she always arrived, which had been true for twelve years now and showed no signs of changing. She had a system and the system was reliable and she did not see the point of reliability that wasn't also consistency. The Ginger Mae opened at seven-fifteen because that was when people wanted coffee. People wanted coffee because the ferry from Cedar Point arrived at seven and the first thing a person wanted after forty minutes on open water was something warm and stationary.

The shop looked the same. It had looked the same for two years now, since they had inherited it, or since Grandma Knapp had died and left it to all three of them equally in a will that had not surprised anyone who knew her, which was everyone on Patchogu Island. The cedar shingles gone silver-grey. The hand-lettered sign. The chalkboard on the sidewalk where Olivia had written, in her own handwriting that was nothing like Grandma's: Tuesday: Corn chowder. Bread today: sourdough.
What was new was the display.

Victoria had done it in March, on a trip to the island that the others hadn't been part of. She had gone down alone, in the off-season, and spent a week in the shop doing the kind of administrative work that accumulated over winters, and while she was there she had built the display. She'd used the glass-top case that used to hold the pastry selection and retired to the storage room, brought it out, cleaned it, and arranged three of Grandma Knapp's recipe notebooks inside it under a sheet of UV-protective glass. Open to pages she had chosen carefully. Next to the case: a small framed card in her own handwriting that said: The notebooks of Ginger Mae Knapp, 1969-2007. She had taken a photograph and sent it to Olivia and Solei without comment.
Olivia had responded: this is good.
Solei had responded: which notebooks did you use?

Victoria had not been sure, at the time, what Solei meant by that. She had assembled the display carefully, the right notebooks, the right pages, the right handwriting on the right card. She had thought she was honoring Grandma Knapp. She had not yet understood that she didn't know, fully, who Grandma Knapp was, and that the not-knowing was the thing worth paying attention to.

She had first begun to understand it the previous October, in a federal building in Jacksonville, sitting across from a supervisory agent who had opened a folder and shown her a black-and-white photograph taken sixty years ago. On the way back to the island, on the ferry, in the cold, with the lights of Cedar Point behind her, she had thought: I have known Grandma Knapp my entire life. I have been wrong about her every day of it. The display was her attempt to look more carefully.

The morning moved the way Tuesday mornings moved on Patchogu in June, without urgency, but with texture. The ferry crowd came through between seven and seven forty-five, people who lived off-island and commuted, people visiting family, two electricians from Cedar Point who always ordered the same thing and never spoke to each other while they did it. By eight the shop had settled into its mid-morning pace: a few tables occupied, the sound of the old refrigerator unit cycling on and cycling off, the smell of the second bread loaf beginning.
Solei came in at eight-ten, sat at the four-top by the window, and didn't say anything until Victoria set a coffee in front of her.
How was the year,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said. Not quite a question.
Productive.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei wrapped both hands around the mug.
I presented at the AIAA conference in January. The paper's being considered for a journal. My advisor said she's never had a first-year student publish.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: She hasn't?
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: No. But she said it in a way that made it clear she found it more alarming than impressive.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Victoria sat down across from her.
And outside of the work?
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Solei considered this with the full seriousness she brought to questions people usually answered quickly.
I made three friends,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: she said.

One of them is exceptional. I found a coffee shop four blocks from the engineering building that makes a passable pour-over, which I'd thought was impossible in that part of Chapel Hill. I ran a half-marathon I hadn't trained for and finished it, which I don't recommend. And I came home.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: She said the last part without emphasis. It was simply the last item on the list.
You came home,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said.
I came home.
Olivia was behind the counter taking inventory with a clipboard, which was how she always spent the lull before nine. She had been listening, as she always listened, without appearing to.
The gutter on the east side is still loose,
spans.speaker: Olivia

spans.text: she said.
I know,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei said.
I called someone in February.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: They never came.
I know. I'll go up myself this week.
Olivia made a note on her clipboard and said nothing else, which was her version of approval.
The woman came in at nine twenty-three.

Victoria was behind the counter running the credit card reconciliation from the previous week, which required the kind of focused, repetitive attention she had learned to give without fully giving, so she saw the woman enter, heard the bell, noted the door, glanced up, and logged her the way she logged everyone: height, approximate age, what she was carrying, whether she looked like she'd been here before.

Height: medium. Age: late thirties, possibly early forties. Carrying: a laptop bag and a water bottle with a university logo that Victoria couldn't read from the counter. She had not been here before. Her shoes said she had walked a distance.

She sat at the table in the back left corner, not the window table, which was the table people chose when they wanted to be seen, but the corner table, which was the table people chose when they wanted to work. She opened the laptop. She ordered chamomile when Solei went over.
Working vacation?
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei asked, which was not a question they usually asked.
The woman looked up. She had the kind of focus that was slightly startling when it turned on you, not unfriendly, but complete.
Research,
she said.
I'm at RTP the rest of the year. I try to take summers somewhere quiet.
You picked a good one,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei said.
That's what I keep hearing.
The woman smiled, went back to her screen.

She stayed for ninety minutes. She was good company in the way solitary, focused people were good company; she took up exactly the space she needed and no more. She refilled her chamomile once. She did not look up from the laptop except to watch the harbor through the window once, briefly, the way people watched things they hadn't expected to find beautiful.
At ten fifty-five, she packed up. She tucked her laptop under her arm, capped the water bottle, came to the register to settle her tab.
And then she stopped.
She was standing at the counter, wallet open, and her eyes had gone to the display case. She looked at it the way you looked at something that had just said your name in a room where no one knew you.

Victoria watched her. Watched the wallet stop moving. Watched the woman's focus narrow to the open page of the middle notebook, a page from October 1972, a bread recipe, Grandma's handwriting in black ink that had faded to brown at the edges.
She paid. She thanked Victoria. She went to leave.
Then she turned back to the display.

She had her phone out. She photographed the left notebook, three shots, adjusting the angle. The middle notebook, two shots. Then, after a pause, the right notebook, which was open to a different year, a different recipe, but the same handwriting in the same faded ink.
She put the phone in her jacket pocket. She said thank you to the middle distance, then went out.
The bell rang.
Victoria stood at the counter and looked at the door.

Solei appeared from the kitchen, carrying a clean dish towel. She had seen it from the back, had been watching through the service window, because Solei watched things through service windows the way other people watched things through windows on trains. The detail registered as she passed.
Did you see that?
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Victoria said.
The photographs.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei leaned against the counter.
She did three separate angles.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: She's done this before. Photographing documents.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Or she knew what she was looking for.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei folded the dish towel with the same precision she applied to everything.
Which three did she photograph?
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: The October '72 one. The June '69. And the winter of '74.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: Solei put the folded towel on the counter. Her expression was the expression she had in her first year on the island, when she looked at something and was not quite ready to tell you what she saw in it. Older now. More certain.
Victoria,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: she said.
I need to look inside those notebooks.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Which ones. There are fifteen of them in the safe.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: All of them.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Victoria looked at the display case. At the bread recipe from October 1972, open under glass. The handwriting. The measurements. The patient, specific instructions for something that rose and browned and fed people for sixty years.
I haven't looked at them,
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: she said.
Since she died, I mean. I looked at them to choose the display. But not, carefully.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: I know.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Grandma said don't go rummaging.
spans.speaker: Victoria

spans.text: She also left you the key,
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Solei said.
She knew you had it. She knew what you'd do with it when the time came.
spans.speaker: Solei

spans.text: Victoria considered that. The supply closet key. The safe. The key to the safe on a small ring, labeled in Grandma's handwriting: recipes. The label she had always thought was simply practical.
Come back tonight,
she said.
After close.
Solei nodded. She picked up the dish towel and went back to the kitchen.

At the four-top by the window, a couple who had been there since nine-thirty were finally gathering their things. One of them called over to ask if there was more bread. There was. Victoria cut it and brought it over and said it was on her, because it was the end of the loaf.
She stood there for a moment after they thanked her, looking at the street through the window, at the specific summer-morning quality of the light.

She thought about the woman. The three angles. The October 1972 notebook under glass. The care with which the photographs had been taken, not tourist casual, not the quick snap of something charming. Something else.
The way you documented evidence.
